text: In writing a life. <break time="0.8s" /> The life narrator and the biographer. <break time="0.8s" /> Engage different kinds of evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> Most biographers incorporate multiple forms of evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> Including historical documents, interviews, and family archives. <break time="0.8s" /> Which they evaluate for validity. <break time="0.8s" /> Relatively few biographers use. <break time="0.8s" /> Their personal memories of their subject. <break time="0.8s" /> As reliable evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> Unless they had a personal relationship. <break time="0.8s" /> To the subject of the biography. <break time="0.8s" /> As a relative, child, friend, or colleague. <break time="0.8s" /> For life narrators, by contrast. <break time="0.8s" /> Personal memories are the primary archival source. <break time="0.8s" /> They may have recourse to other kinds of sources. <break time="0.8s" /> Letters, journals, photographs, conversations. <break time="0.8s" /> And to their knowledge of a historical moment. <break time="0.8s" /> But the usefulness of such evidence for their stories. <break time="0.8s" /> Lies in the ways. <break time="0.8s" /> In which they employ that evidence. <break time="0.8s" /> To support, supplement, or offer commentary. <break time="0.8s" /> On their personalized acts of remembering. <break time="0.8s" /> In autobiographical narratives. <break time="0.8s" /> Imaginative acts of remembering. <break time="0.8s" /> Always overlap with such rhetorical acts. <break time="0.8s" /> As assertion, justification, judgment, conviction, and questioning.
